utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon once again, sir. You may already be aware of it, but again as I have said before it's my duty to remind you that the declaration you took at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth, still binds you at this stage. Good afternoon, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My condolences.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Remind me, are we with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, we're with me, Your Honour, for just a little while longer, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Yeah, the whole morning escaped me. Here we are at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just have some more questions for you today; I hope it won't take too much longer. To begin with, on Friday you testified that you knew Goran Opacic personally, and I was wondering if you could describe him for us physically, how tall he was, what colour his hair was, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew Goran Opacic personally, and his family, too. His brothers and his father; I didn't know his mother. He is about 1.80 metres tall. He completed a political high school or a police high school, and he was a police officer in Sinj or in Split. As the relevant events unfolded in Krajina, he returned there. He hails from a village in Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Focusing just for a second and getting on sort of his physical characteristics. What colour hair did he have?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was black, but his hair was closely clipped most of the time. He had a crew cut, I believe, and that's why I don't really remember the colour of his hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. And just one more question about this. Do you remember if he wore glasses?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wore glasses after he got wounded. He's seriously disabled now. It was toward the end of the war. I don't think he wore any at the outset of the war. In 1993 he was seriously wounded and his eyesight was impaired and that was when he started wearing glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I see. Did this -- what kind of other wounds did he have? Was he still able to walk around and things like that, or was it just his eyes that were wounded mostly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was able to walk around. I believe that it was only his eyes that were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. You also testified that Opacic was something of a bragger who tried to make himself into a hero, but that in reality he -- I think you said he ran away whenever there was a dangerous situation. Is that right? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, listen. Opacic was one of the first police officers to come to the territory of Krajina from Croatia, as far as I know, and he was quite highly rated and respected by his peers on the police force. He has a very athletic physique, he's very dexterous and intelligent, and as such he managed to win the confidence and trust of his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. For instance, did you know that the RSK Ministry of the Interior awarded Goran Opacic a security service plaque due to his "demonstrated bravery, self-sacrifice, or exceptional contribution to the successful operation of the internal affairs service"?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's a quote from Exhibit 462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you know about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you know whether Goran Opacic was later given an award in 1997 by the chief of the Serbian State Security Services, Jovica Stanisic? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that either. I don't remember. I didn't work for these services. Goran Opacic spent most of his service during wartime on the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me just show you a clip. Actually, it's something that's on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So if we could all turn to our regular e-court screens and we'll broadcast the Sanction. Hopefully this will work. Okay. Let's go ahead and play the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "To mark the day of the special operations unit of the Republic of Serbia state security, the chief of the Republic of Serbia State Security Service, Mr. Jovica Stanisic, will present awards. Radomir Ratkovic. Sima Ratkovic. Nikola Pupovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to go ahead and fast-forward a little bit, but there are more awards to people being handed out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Miomir Popovic. Goran Opacic."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, can you confirm that that's Goran Opacic there who just gave three kisses with Jovica Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Goran Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. There he receives a reward. And I'll just fast-forward to one last part of the same clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to recognise any of the men there or the men besides Jovica Stanisic, who we've already seen?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen Jovica Stanisic in person, only through such media broadcasts. As for the others, I am not familiar with them because I was not a member of the police force and did not have occasion to socialise with people working for the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. Thank you. Just a couple more seconds of this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we move off. Who is Jovica Stanisic there? I know we saw him a little bit earlier but it was fast moving and those of us who are slow on the uptake couldn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It appears from the dialogue that he's in the person in the middle, Your Honour, and he's about to speak and I think that will clarify it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We have now actually given out the highest awards that can be earned in the work of this kind, and these are the awards for valour. Each one of you that received this award, be it Opacic in the Knin area, or Djurica in the Banja area, and even that story about us as men who tried to help their people ... each one of them is the same, particularly in terms of the way it came about. But in essence, it speaks of the heroism of our people and what we have put into our unit and into those who will carry on the tradition of this unit."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just ask a question for clarification?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How is Opacic's name spelled, with a T or a C in the middle? It has been spelled differently on this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, can you clarify that for us? How do you spell Goran Opacic's surname?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: O-p-a-c-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are we able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Rewind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe in the transcript, which is a transcript that someone -- I don't actually know in the OTP or in the language part made the transcript, and I know that it does have a T in there but I believe that's just -- they didn't hear it correctly. He was able to confirm that it was the person that we're interested in. I can go back to it if you'd like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to know whether the person whose name is spelled with a C who's referred to being in Knin, is it a different person, Opacic and not Opatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I believe it is the same person who we saw and that the witness identified as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could this please be admitted into evidence? It's just this clip that we've seen with the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The clip with the transcript is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And we're done with that then. It can be taken off of our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, at the end of the day on Friday, I was showing you a few documents, and I just want to show you a couple more. And the first one is Exhibit 614.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could please see that on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, this is another document like some of the ones we saw last week, which is based on an interview with someone who claims to have participated in the combat activities in the village of Skabrnja. And as you see in that first paragraph, this person says that he saw members of the TO and volunteers killing civilians in the village. I just want to point you to a couple of particular passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down, please. That's perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see there in the first photograph in quotes there, sir, in the second sentence it says -- actually, I don't need to read it out specifically. But it says there that members of the TO and volunteers brought a group of about 20 civilians from a basement. It says: "One of them had a PAP." What does that refer to, do you know, Mr. Lakic, a PAP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semi-automatic rifle. I believe that's what it means. That's just a type of infantry weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And then this -- the document continues to say that they -- they took a person behind the BOV and they shot him. Then they brought an old woman and two old men and made them lie on the ground and shot them in the back of the head. In the next little paragraph they talk about two men ages 35 and 45 being interrogated and then shot. Sir, did you have any information about TO members participating in incidents such as are described in this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about this document - let's call it a document because this is simply a note, it doesn't qualify as a document - some four or five months after the action. This is an interview between a security officer or a security organ and his source. I don't know who the source is. I was never familiarised with any such situations as the one described here or with these persons being participants because they could not possibly have been in Skabrnja at the time. And this isn't something I'm telling you that I -- because I heard about it. I'm telling you because it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, okay, that was going to be my next question. Having seen all the documents that we reviewed on Friday as well as this document, is it still your position that TO members did not participate in the fighting in Skabrnja on the 18th of November and did not commit any crimes there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only am I stating this, I am quite positive about it. Except for the medical unit and the minibus that was used for evacuating the population, not a single unit of mine was there on that date, the 18th of November, in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You mentioned the medical unit. Do you remember who was part of that medical unit, how many people it had, and what were their names, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the establishment of the Territorial Defence, the medical unit had seven to eight men who worked in 24-hour shifts, or rather, they worked in shifts around-the-clock. They were always on the stand-by. Three or four of them were active on that day, and the commander of the medical unit was a lady, Nada Pupovac. At that point in time, she was in the area of Skabrnja and she took part in providing medical assistance to the population and in facilitating their evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I'd like you to look at one more document with regard to the Skabrnja operations, it's Exhibit 107.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see that on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And actually, Mr. Lakic, this is a document we looked at briefly before. It's the officer's notebook of Mr. Bogunovic. So I'll just bring that back on our screen for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Has the one been a document as an evidence piece or is it just -- 614, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was already previously admitted, so I'm sorry I didn't mention that. Could we turn, please, to the page 02006878. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And focus first at the top left-hand corner, Mr. Lakic, and again I know that it may be hard to read this a little bit because it's handwritten but ... At the very top there you see that it gives the date 20th of November, 1991, and it refers to the analysis of the mopping-up operation. And it looks like it says NSZG. This refers, doesn't it, to analysis of the operation against Nadin, Skabrnja, and Zemunik Gornje. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this abbreviation means. I've never used it. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm just going to point to a couple different passages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt? My document ends at 6869, and when I go back to the source I get the handwritten one which I think is --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, it should be on page 3 of the English. I apologise for not saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, we may have to scroll down just a bit, but you see -- you can see it there the name Djurica. Yeah, that's fine right there. And actually it's the next entry below that. Can you read the next underlined name there? You have Djurica and then some sort of bullet points and then another name. Can you read that one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovic or something or other. It's quite illegible. But I don't recall there being a Jovic. Or perhaps Dobic in Latin script. I wasn't familiar with all the JNA commanding officers and their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. It's one that I'm also unable to decipher.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think if we'll just focus on the last two and see if you find this. It says there: "Arsons and looting less than in some of the earlier operations and there were cases of uncivilised killings." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that, yes, if that's what it really says because I can't make out all the words.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, if that is in fact what it says, this would suggest that at least the JNA command on the 20th of November, 1991, was already aware of crimes committed in Skabrnja or Nadin or Zemunik Gornji; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they must have been aware of that or they must have known because the information to the effect that there was killing and that there were victims reached us quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could now look at the right-hand side of this page and actually scroll up to the top a little bit, please. That's fine right there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see there, sir, where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On what page will that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: On the fourth page in English. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lakic, you see there it refers to an analysis made by the commanding staff, and then you see Bosko Drazic, and then the next entry down is Zoran Lakic, refers to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, in the English it says Zoran Lekic, but I think there's just a difficulty in deciphering the handwritten script there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember attending a meeting around this time, around the 20th of November, with Drazic and other commanders who were involved in the Skabrnja operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a great many meetings for various reasons. This is probably one of the working meetings of the JNA to which we were invited.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let me just focus you on a couple of the bullet points under your name there. The second one says: "Ten days ago Drazic took one platoon from the TO units." Do you know what that's a reference to? What does it mean by he took one platoon from the TO units?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically I don't know what it refers to as far as Drazic goes. But you have to know that on the 1st of November the Territorial Defence and the Yugoslav People's Army and the TO staff were completely transformed, restructured. There were structural changes in units. On the 1st of November, the TO brigade was set up, too, under the command of active officers of the JNA. Now, what this specifically refers to, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Look at the next bullet point down. It's also a little hard to read, but I think it says: "Three civilians were transported from the point 16 and killed in," and then there's a word that is illegible, "needs to be investigated." Do you remember raising this at a meeting, that you knew that three civilians had been transported from a point 16 and then killed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received information to the effect that three civilians, or, rather, persons wearing civilians clothes -- so we had that information. And I asked that inquiries be made as to the whereabouts of these people. I didn't know who had taken them away, and I really don't know what their fate was. But I did ask for the matter to be inquired into.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so by this time you already had information about civilians being killed in Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received such information only, or rather, only detailed information after the sanitization of the -- of the ground. It was only after that that I received information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you must have had some information --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just find out. If the information is not detailed, it doesn't tell you of any crimes being committed? If you get a very cryptic report that three civilians have been taken by the -- some of your commanders, your troops, and killed, unless it is detailed, that doesn't tell you that people have been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My medical corps commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: By this time, by this time, you were aware that three civilians had been transported and killed. Whether or not the report you got was detailed, whether or not the report you got was before or after sanitization, but you heard this information. Is it not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't receive information about three civilians having been killed. I merely received information that their whereabouts were not known, and that's when I asked that this be inquired into. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, the problem before you continue is that you're now talking about whereabouts. This report talks about killing. And this is the part of the report that comes under your name. "Three civilians were transported from the point 16 and killed ... needs to be investigated." This is -- there is a fundamental difference between "and killed" and not know the whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We received information that allegedly they had been killed, but nobody was able to confirm this. For this reason, I requested that the matter be investigated because we had unconfirmed information of their -- of their having been killed; however, we didn't know where they ended up, what became of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once again, that's a departure from this report. This report doesn't say they were allegedly killed; it says they were killed. You are now introducing "alleged." What needs to be investigated may perhaps be who did it, but it seems that the report is definitive as to what happened to them. They were killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know why I asked that the matter be investigated, and that's according to this report. I can't think at the moment of any other reason for me asking that it be investigated other than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just suggested to you the other reason could be to investigate who killed, not whether the killing did in fact take place.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is minutes of a working meeting. It's a very abbreviated form without full-blown sentences. I probably said investigations into the facts should be made and that perpetrators should be detected, but this is -- these are minutes which were just jotted down. I don't remember the whole story in detail, but it was clear that something had to be done to determine the facts and to take measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I appreciate that very much. I appreciate that very much. But having said that, you would agree with me that if at the time of writing these notes there was no certainty about what became of these people, that uncertainty would have been reflected in the minutes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I presume that it should have been in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It should have been put this way; is that what you say? Sorry. I presume ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if it should have been in this way, then that way can only mean that they were killed and that you knew at the time that they were killed. Are we agreed on that? You may not have known of the circumstances under which they died, but that they died you seem to have known. According to this minute; I'm not saying that the minute is right. I'm saying if the minute is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, at that moment I was in possession of unconfirmed information; it wasn't confirmed. I didn't know where, whom, or when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Okay. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, earlier -- in the last few minutes I think you started to explain something and you mentioned your medical corps commander, and I just wondered if you wanted to give us some information about that or something that you heard from your medical corps commander. I'm not sure, but is there something you wanted to add about that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who was the person giving me information. Under chaotic circumstances on the 18th, I spoke to tens of people and received information from all over the place. I solely relied on information of my subordinates from the commander of the medical unit, and the first information was received by the commander of the medical detachment that there were victims, among them civilians. JNA then blockaded the whole place. They conducted their investigation. They determined the facts, and only in subsequent days I could receive further information. I was in no position to achieve or get first-hand information only through intermediaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. What was the name of the medical corps commander who you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Nada Pupovac, commander of the medical unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Turning your attention back now to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Still on page 4 in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you skip down a couple of bullet points you see there it says the OB, or the security organ, "should take steps to identify those who committed crimes, robberies and barbarities." And then the next one says: "There are individuals who do not deserve," and the next line, "however, we do not have other soldiers for such operations." So, sir, it's clear from this entry as well that you knew at this time that there had been crimes, robberies, and barbarities in Skabrnja; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew from my commander, yes, I knew, from the medical squad commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And then the second-to-last bullet point you say that Rekenji did a wrong thing in Polaca. And I'm just wondering, is that a reference to the fighting in Polaca in May 1991 or is that -- or can you explain what the reference is there to Polaca, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Captain Rekenji of -- ethnic Hungarian, Rekenji. I don't know what this refers to. He was a commander of the tank unit. I presume that we discussed damage inflicted on buildings and facilities in Polaca inflicted by JNA tanks. And this refers to Rekenji; he's an ethnic Hungarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page in B/C/S, please, and it's also the next page, page 5, in the English, Your Honours. And I'm looking for where Lieutenant Tadic speaks. There we go, on the right-hand side. Thank you very much. It's wonderful to have an usher who can navigate through the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, look at what Lieutenant Tadic says there. And I'll just read through a couple of these and follow along with me. He says: "Special units did not mop up the houses in front of the tank. They were all wearing Chetnik insignia, and they cannot be used in any other future operation. When Cedo KV tried to stop the killing, they wanted to kill him." And then a few bullet points down it says: "He kills a man as soon as he sees him. He kills dogs." And then another bullet point down: "Some of the soldiers in the company started looting." Sir, were you privy to this kind of information, this kind of feedback from the operation about people wearing Chetnik insignia and killing people upon sight, the difficulty of people to intervene, were you aware of this kind of information?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Lieutenant Tadic, I don't know him. He's probably an officer of the JNA. I never had occasion to meet him. I don't recall him, to tell you from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could -- I think we could turn to the next page, please, 6880, it's the same page in English, and go to the top left-hand corner. It's a continuation of what Lieutenant Tadic is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If you look down to about the fourth bullet point it says: "Only one man was wearing Ustasha uniform. More than 20 killed. They were about to kill a woman and a child, saying: 'Ustasha bastards.' The MP soldier did the same." And then if you skip down a couple it says: "Lieutenant-Colonel Dabic was present during maltreatment of civilians. When I ask him: What do you think you're doing? He asks me what my nationality is." Mr. Lakic, do you remember things like this being discussed among the commanders? Did you hear about incidents like these?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Lieutenant-Colonel Dabic. We knew what happened. We had preliminary information without any investigation having taken place a couple of days after the event. The terminology that was used, referring to the Croatian army and the terminology of Croatian army towards us, dates back from World War II. No wonder that we referred to them in this way and that they referred to us in accordance with their terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to stay with this document, but I'm going to ask you some questions that go a little later in time because this notebook continues. But before I do, is it correct that after the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, some inhabitants remained in Skabrnja. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really know that. This is not within the territory of the municipality of Benkovac, and this was outside my zone of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So if I were to put to you that between about the time of the operation up until February 1992, that more than 20 people went missing or were killed from Skabrnja, I guess -- will you be able to offer any information about that, or is that something you just don't know about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 18th when my tasks were exclusively to secure my territory, after November 18th, 1991, with reference to the Skabrnja territory, I had no tasks, any responsibilities, and -- nor did I gather any information from that territory. I was solely tasked with securing the territory of the municipality of Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just point you to one particular passage and then we can be done with this document for today. It's -- the page in B/C/S is 02006900, and it's an entry for the 10th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's an page 7 in the English version, Your Honours. Yeah, there it is on the -- right there on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, under the entry for the 10th of December, 1991, the third bullet point says: "In Skabrnja TO members kill one elderly person each day." Did you receive information about people, elderly people or otherwise, being killed in Skabrnja in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Skabrnja action, seven days after that, maybe ten - I cannot be specific - duty to give that territory was given to the brigade of TO, not my unit. The brigade of TO was an autonomous unit under the command of the JNA and led by officers of the JNA. So it had nothing to do with me, the TO of Benkovac. That brigade was mobile, and the Lieutenant Pavo Samardzic -- Lieutenant-Colonel Pavo Samardzic was the commander. And it had nothing to do with the TO which was there to defend the civilians. As opposed to this brigade, my units were not mobile, which means they were connected with the territory of their villages. That brigade was mobile and they operated in certain areas, but I do not have any information about its operations. I believe hat this could be the brigades I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. We're done with that document. And I just have one more document to ask you about, sir. Before I do, in 1995 did you have meetings with representatives of the European Community Monitoring Mission, specifically around April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, with the representatives of the UN, European Community and all structures of the UN, I maintained daily contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me show you one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The ERN is R0243812, if we could see that on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lakic, I'm sorry, this is a document in the English so I apologise for that. But I'll read out to you the part that we're concerned with. And what the document is, as we wait for it to come on our screen, it's an ECMM daily report from -- dated the 26th of April, 1995. Oh, wow, we have it in B/C/S. I didn't realise that. That's great. So you can follow along with me more easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down, please, to the first big paragraph, "Political Situation," exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: First of all, you'll see, sir, about the second or third sentence it says: "There will never be a way of reintegration of Croats into the RSK, but there's still Croats living and working in the area of Benkovac," and you talk about Croatian officers and many soldiers. Well -- and actually, I'll just ask you a question about a different part. If you look further down --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In fact, could we go to the next page of the translation, please. It's still on the same page in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I hope this is clear. Maybe it's a sentence that went from one page to the next. But there is a sentence that says: "He is afraid" -- and it's talking about you. "He is afraid about a new war with Croatia, but if it is necessary, the ARSK will use heavy weapons they never used before, rocket-launchers to reach Zagreb and Split and special chemical weapons." Do you remember making such remarks to the ECMM, sir, about -- that if it was necessary that the SVK would use rocket-launchers to reach Zagreb and Split?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who this gentleman who drafted the report is quoting. At that time was chief of police. My weapons and my knowledge about the weapons of the Army of Serbian RSK were non-existent. I did not know whether they had such weaponry or not. I am sure, I am certain, that I never stated this. This is beyond question. It says "officers of the army," as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yeah, well, let's go back to the first page. I'm sorry, I went too quickly and maybe I didn't make this clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could go to the first page of the translation and scroll down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you see in the first paragraph, sir, it says that they had a meeting -- arranged a meeting with the chief of the militia in Benkovac, Zoran Lakic, and his deputy Gojko Calac which was held in a friendly atmosphere. So that's a reference to you, correct, as you said as head of the police. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was head of the public security station at Benkovac at the time, but I am sure that I never discussed chemical weapons or rockets because still I don't know what we had at our disposal. Maybe this was a provocative question of the person I discussed these things with, whether we had those weapons or not. But I'm sure that I never said that because we -- it states here we discussed something that I did not know anything about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, thank you for answering my questions. No further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Black. Mr. Milovancevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since that before my question we had your answer of my learned friend concerning this document, 993, I would like to -- for this exhibit, 993, to be brought back on the screens. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: -- discussion with the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's not overlap in our questions and answers because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall that possible discussion on military issues, as you explained to the Prosecutor, was in your opinion in the form of a provocative question by the ECMM people.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this document before you?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look at the bottom of the page, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The second sentence in this paragraph there is the following text which reads: "Head of the police asserted firmly that Germany and the US of A are guilty with regard to the situation in the RSK. It will never be possible for the Croatians to reintegrate into the RSK, but there are still Croats who live and work in the area of Benkovac. For instance, in the ARSK there are six to eight Croatian officers and a large number of soldiers." Can you see this text?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That's April 1995. Is that correct, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This piece of information as interpreted by the ECMM, that Croatians within the RSK are part of the Army of RSK, this is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. I know some of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We no longer need this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will broach another subject. Do you recall when the Prosecutor showed you some photographs showing facilities destroyed in Skabrnja; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall an answer put to you -- a question put to you as to when you visited Skabrnja with regard to the destruction?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At a certain point, maybe you remember that, you started saying that you visited Skabrnja in 1992, and then His Honour Moloto interrupted you saying that you are being examined concerning 1992 and 1993, not 1991. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You visited Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991, as you stated that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you visit Skabrnja after that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, the end of 1992, when units of JNA, TO were re-established into the brigade of border police sometime in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, in November 1992, did you notice the condition of the buildings, houses, in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my first impression was that the damage to buildings were the same as one year earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spoke about these -- about the destruction and you said that the damage was the same as one year earlier. Could you describe summarily what kind of damage was that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damage to the roofs from mortar shells, maybe 1 or 2 square metres of roof tiles. There were holes in walls from artillery and tank fire, but we had information that Croatian forces from the direction of Prkos they would shell JNA while it was in Skabrnja in 1992. But these -- the level of damage was not drastic. The damage was not the same as was shown on the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall in trying to answer the Prosecutor's questions you mentioned some battles in 1993. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did these battles take place and what bearing had that on Skabrnja, could you explain that, in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 23rd of January, 1993, in the wider area of Northern Dalmatia there was an overall aggression of Croatian forces against the Serbian territory in Northern Dalmatia, whereby Croatian forces, units of Croatian army and other units at their disposal, attacked the territory of the municipalities of Benkovac, Obrovac, and Gracac, and partly the Knin municipality territory. The main axis of their attack was the territory of the Benkovac municipality, the axis of airport at Zemunik towards Smiljcic and Debelo Brdo the other axis of their attack was Zeleni Hrast, Islam Grcki, Kasic, Smiljcic, Debelo Brdo. One of the axis of their attack touched upon the territory of Skabrnja, and in the battles, very fierce battles that unfolded over the next one month or so at the point of contact with Croatian forces, there was such intense shelling that even fortified buildings would have been extensively damaged. So these were the battles of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the attack of the Croatian forces against this territory. Did this attack have a common name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I can't remember the term. I used to know it, but I cannot recall it right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was that attack directed at the area of Maslenica?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right, Maslenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have Exhibit 30 on our screens, please. This is a document concerning photographs that were taken on the 25th of November, 1991. I have either provided the wrong number or you may have been mistaken. Can I ask the assistance of my learned friend Mr. Black concerning the number of the folder containing photographs that were made by the security station. I believe you used that same folder in your cross-examination. I must have written the wrong number.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think it's Exhibit 270.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor showed you some of the photographs made in Skabrnja - and we have the document here and I will have a couple of questions concerning that as well - as -- can you tell us in your opinion when was the serious extent of the damage you can see in the photographs inflicted?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been inflicted after 1992. In the course of 1993, when there was fierce fighting and destruction on a large scale on both sides, because Skabrnja changed hands, it was at one point under the control of the Serb forces and others of the Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please take a look at some of the photographs here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, your opposite number is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. There may have been confusion. 270 were photographs that were taken by the Benkovac security station, and that's why I mentioned that one. The exhibit with photographs of destruction which I showed to the witness is Exhibit 272. So I apologise for the confusion. I'm not exactly sure which one counsel wants to use, but those are the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel, which one do you want to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm grateful to my learned friend Mr. Black. I was only interested in the cover page of this document, the document that we have on our screens right now. I will not be needing it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you read out the text for us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Massacre committed by the Chetnik formations on the civilian victims on the 18th of November, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And below that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Copies out of the original photo documentation discovered in an abandoned automobile of the Zastava 101 make in Benkovac on the 6th of April, 1996."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that among the photo documentation that was found in the disused automobile there were also photographs shown to you by the Prosecutor of both the victims and buildings destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the subject of the report is the massacre committed on the civilians by Chetnik units on the 18th of November, 1991. What sort of Chetnik units are being referred to here, can you tell us anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, see, this is the terminology dating back to World War II. The Serb side referred to the Croatian side as Ustasha most often; and they responded in equal measure, by referring to all the members of the Serb forces as Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, just for my own clarification, that previous question you said, that's at line 16: "Do you recall that among the photo documentation that was found in the disused automobile there were also photographs shown to you by the Prosecutor of both the victims and buildings destroyed?" Were these among the same package or are these two separate exhibits actually? I thought Mr. Black talked of Exhibit 270 and 272. This, I think, is 270 that is on the screen; and the one that contains photos of destroyed property is 272. He can correct me if I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No, that's exactly right, Your Honour, and they are two separate exhibits with separate origins, as testified by witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just the question where you say "among," "among the documentation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you are correct. It was a mistake on my part. I fully accept what you said. These were two separate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I misrepresented that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that in the last answer by the witness he said: "Referring to all the members of the Serb forces, including the JNA as Chetniks."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the following. We would find interesting the following. According to this report, the photo documentation was found in an abandoned automobile of the Zastava 101 make in Benkovac on the 6th of April, 1996. Do you know the -- whether the photo documentation compiled by the SUP Benkovac in the 1991 to 1995 period or, rather, when this photo documentation left the area or until what point was it in the hands of the SUP Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the 4th of August, 1995, that all the staff of the SUP Benkovac left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that the documentation belonging to the SUP Benkovac was found in this car almost a year later, in 1996. You see that here?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as the photographs depicting damaged buildings are concerned, and I mean those buildings that suffered extensive damage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to do this to you, Mr. Milovancevic. Once again, can you just direct me where it says that the documentation belongs to the SUP of Benkovac. You -- we haven't paged through. We are still on page 1 of this document, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not commenting on the cover page here; I was, rather, referring to Mr. Black's question wherein he referred to the photo documentation that he said was made by the SUP Benkovac in 1991. And this was the same documentation that was found in the abandoned car. I wasn't specifically referring to the document we have on our screens. We can go into that document, but I was merely referring the witness back to the questions that had been put to him and the answers that he gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your question was: "It says here that the documentation belonging to the SUP Benkovac was found in this car almost a year later, in 1996." When you say "it says here," what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're right. This is not what the cover page reads. Allow me, please, to rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was making inferences. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: It says here that this is a copy of the original photo documentation retrieved from an abandoned car of the Zastava 101 make in Benkovac on the 6th of April, 1996. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor showing you photographs as part of the documentation that was authored in the SUP Benkovac in 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is my question: Can you rule out the possibility that the damage inflicted on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, is shown in this photo documentation in the condition in which they were in 1993 after the Maslenica operation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say that the two conditions in which the buildings could be found were incomparable --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection, because I think what's happening here is Defence counsel is conflating two things. He's taking the date from one exhibit and he's transferring that date on to another exhibit. And witnesses came and testified about where these came from. It's clear that the photos of destruction didn't come from the Benkovac SUP, they don't bear the stamp of the Benkovac SUP, as do the photos in Exhibit 270. In this question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Having said that, can you just give me the sense of that question. I don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understood the question as trying to show that because Exhibit 270 was found in a car in 1996, Exhibit 272 must have been somehow doctored with or tampered with or the date of it is uncertain. That's why I object, because it's confusing two exhibits and the dates regarding two exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Milovancevic, there is a physical impossibility in my mind to your question. Can you rule out the possibility that the damage inflicted on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, is shown in this photo documentation in the condition in which they were in 1993 after the Maslenica operation? How can a damage that is inflicted on -- in 1991 appear in a condition of 1993? Before you answer my question, maybe you can respond to the objection. Do you want to take a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps that would be convenient, and then we can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Remember the objection when we come back. Court adjourned. Come back at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's my turn --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I have to respond to what my learned friend Mr. Black said. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My apologies. You don't have anything to apologise for, Mr. Milovancevic, I must apologise. Thank you. I'm very sorry. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my colleague Mr. Black is right as far as these exhibits are concerned. These are two sets of photographs. I withdraw my earlier question. I will rephrase it fully by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lakic, you do remember the Prosecutor showing you a set of photographs taken in the area of Skabrnja. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you also recall another set of photographs which dealt with the extent of damaged inflicted on Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that in 1992 you were in Skabrnja and you saw the condition of the buildings there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is my following question: Is it possible that the damage to be seen in the photographs shown to you by the Prosecutor was inflicted in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mostly certainly in 1993 and the years to follow, in the actions in 1994 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the Prosecutor asking you about whether the Croatian MUP forces were in Skabrnja on the 18th of November, 1991? This is one of the questions, too.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which armed units on the 18th of November, 1991, in the area of Yugoslavia and in the area of Croatia - therefore, in the area of Skabrnja - constituted regular armed formations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The regular armed formation in the Republic of Croatia at the time was the Yugoslav People's Army officially speaking. Therefore -- also as well as the TO. The -- Croatia started establishing its armed formations, which was contrary to the federal laws and regulations governing armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How would you qualify the formations with which clashes occurred on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were irregular formations, paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the Prosecutor asking you about a document which is generally called the Zadar Agreement; that is to say, the agreement between the JNA representatives and the Croatian representatives in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor showing you one of the items of the agreement, I believe it was item 11, although I don't -- I may be mistaken.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the Zadar Agreement. This is Exhibit 990; that was at least how I noted it down. I may be mistaken again. Do you recall seeing the text of this document yesterday? You read out the title of it as well.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was on Friday. Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for correcting me. That was on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please scroll down to see the items, scroll down a bit more, please. Yes, that is fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page are we looking at in the English version, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is page 1 of the document. We are interested in the very beginning of the document. The passage at the top, can we see the beginning of it. Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you read out the first paragraph, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 9th of October, 1991, at the Zemunik military airport, representatives met of the command of the Knin Corps, commander of the Zadar garrison, and representatives of the Zadar Municipal Assembly and command for the defence of the Zadar region concerning the joint obligation toward an absolute cease-fire and ceasing of all military operations, lifting the blockade of the town of Zadar and military facilities and pulling out of manpower, technical, materiel, and combat resources of the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please read out the sentence below the main heading. I will refer you to it. Below the text that you read out it says: "The agreement implies the exercise of the following joint obligations." Please read out item 4.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 4: "Remove forthwith all physical obstacles such as minefields and barricades erected by the units of the armed forces of the Croatian army and JNA units."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us scroll down a bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down. My interpreter is struggling to keep pace, gentlemen. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please read out items 5, 6, and 7 of the agreement, but please read at a slower pace so that the interpreters can follow.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Item 5: "On the contact line, on the line of engagement, and around military facilities in the town of Zadar and the surroundings, disengage forces which -- to a distance which will, depending on the lay of the terrain and the level of settlements there, will exclude mutual friction and activity. The command for the defence of the Zadar region shall be duty-bound to secure military facilities from any activities from armed formations, groups, and individuals. "6. Freedom of movement shall be secured for all members of the armed forces of the SFRY and members of their families." Item 7: "Introduce right away all PTT connections in all military -- or restore all PTT connections to all military facilities and dwellings of the -- their staff and make sure that their units and facilities of the armed forces of the SFRY have water, electricity, food, and other necessary supplies, which will be adequate in terms of the situation in the town of Zadar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the last provision of the agreement I would like you to read is item 8.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 8: "Make sure that pull-out of all the materiel and combat resources of the JNA can be carried out smoothly as well as the evacuation of all of the private property of the persons moving out of Zadar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall the Prosecutor asking you whether you know that such an agreement between the Croatian side and the JNA forces was reached in early October 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor asking you whether the agreement was in fact acted upon; and in the context of that, he showed you a document referring to some 260 trucks that pulled out military equipment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whether what was agreed upon on the 9th of October, 1991, between the Croatian side and the JNA, was it enforced when it comes to Zadar, the Zemunik airport, and the area that you were in?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor asking you what was the real reason of the intervention in Skabrnja or the conflict in Skabrnja? Was it an attack against the largest Croatian village to send a signal to other Croatian villages and inhabitants; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please take --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us take a look -- and this document is no longer needed. So let's take a look at Prosecution 65 ter document 2066 or Exhibit 785. Let it be retrieved on the e-court. That is supposed to be a report of the 9th Corps command from 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read out in the top left corner who is the author of the document.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the 9th Corps commander, strictly confidential, number 696-1, dated 20th of November, 1991, headquarters at Knin. The addressee is the VPO command and the 5th Military District command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we scroll down, please. You can stop here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you in this document, in the second paragraph under item 1, read out the text of that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "On no occasions so far, despite our insistence, members of the ECMM have enabled representatives of our command and command of the Naval District to visit barracks, facilities, and families of the members of the armed forces of the SFRY that have been in total -- subject to a total blockade for several months now. Almost nothing has been done to lift the blockade of the barracks and dislocated facilities and to allow normal supply of same moving around the cities of Sibenik and Split and to guarantee basic human rights and create minimum conditions for their existence."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I should ask you to read out from this document something from item 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please scroll down so that we see the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The first two lines, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Item 3: "Also we state that combat activities have not ceased, combat activities against our facilities. We would like to stress the most recent case of fire being aimed at the Rade Koncar barracks in Sibenik during the night 19th and 20th November, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the past four days, the Zemunik airport has been the target of continued attacks from the Croatian side which result in damage to invaluable technical equipment and people are being injured."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just so that the -- this document is dated 20th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go to the last page of this document, page 3 in the B/C/S version, to see who this -- who signed this document. It's 041-4439 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, it's in front of you. Who signed this?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General-Major Vladimir Vukovic, the commander, signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, who did he command?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Vladimir Vukovic was the commander of the 9th Corps, which was headquartered in Knin, the 9th Corps of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know about the situation out on the ground and around the Zemunik airport, does this document reflect reality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you stick to your answer to the Prosecutor's and my question about what were the reasons for the Skabrnja action?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stick to my statement in full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to the fighting in Skabrnja on the 18th and 19th of November, 1991, do you recall the Prosecutor showing you a report signed by the then-Lieutenant Ernest Radjen about the sanitization of the terrain; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, given that you are a reserve officer and that you were engaged in war, could you explain what in military terms the sanitization of the area means.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In military terms, the term "sanitization" implies physical removal of remains after a military action, remains of the killed members of both sides, of animals, everything, and of equipment so that it -- it is prevented for equipment to be further destroyed. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall the Prosecutor showing you certain items of Ernest Radjen's report, items 4, 6, 9, 10, 12, 13?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which refer to civilian victims. Could you see from these items that apart from civilians that there were killed members of the ZNG or MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In combat situation, what would it mean to you that civilians and armed personnel are inhabiting the same space and area -- what consequences would it lead to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In armed and military operations, armed personnel may use civilians as -- for protection. In concrete terms, in street fighting, armed combat within settlements a soldier who may be captured uses civilians to manoeuvre himself out of that particular area. This may be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this allowed? Is it in keeping with morality and customs of war standards?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Use of civilians to these purposes is by no means allowed; I'm certain of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Can I ask a question here. You have said it's not allowed. How would the other side be required to behave under the customs and laws in relation to war, having seen a situation where the enemy seizes civilians and uses them as a shield in order to manoeuvre the way -- or for some reason, what is the duty in those circumstances? What's the right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in all these actions, to my knowledge, actions of that type, of that type, and fights in villages and towns and cities, what is required is to leave some time for the civilians to withdraw. In this specific case, ample time was left for the civilians to withdraw because more than 1500 civilians of Skabrnja withdrew in the direction of Zadar without any consequences. So these civilians either willingly stayed behind or were members -- were used by members of the ZNG as a human shield. They could have evacuated as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: That's precisely what I'm saying. Having used them as human shields, what was the other side supposed to do in the circumstances in order to satisfy the customs and laws of war? Could you respond by firing at the ZNG when they were using the civilians as shields, or under the circumstances should you avoid returning fire or attacking under those circumstances? Or are you saying that you're allowed to because of the fact that you have given a time for evacuation, and that time-limit is passed and evacuation has not taken place in relation to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only justified answer to your question would be that those civilians who stayed behind with the members of the armed forces of Croatia did that on their own volition or pursuant to a command of the armed forces of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Let's assume that they were acting under the command of the armed forces of Croatia, let's assume that they weren't voluntary.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what I would have done. I did not command that action. But I think that I would not allow any fire being opened against civilians if I were in such a position, I mean I personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: You're speaking tactically really, of what you would do in the heat of the moment out there on the field in the situation, but what I was trying to get from you further is what you would be required to do, what is the right way to behave and strategically conduct the war under those circumstances, as opposed to what would not be permissible. If you think you have nothing further to add, but I really wanted a bit more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had at my disposal the information that all these civilians opened fire; even women opened fire at us. So if a civilian stayed behind with military personnel and opened fire, then all of them are soldiers. If a civilian were to be abused, I believe that I would not go through with such orders if I were ordered so by my superiors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I take it that you're not able to answer, to tell me what the situation ought to be? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I take a slightly different point on this topic. When this question was first put to you, it came as a hypothetical situation. If you look at page 41, line 10, the question was: "In combat situation, what would it mean to you that civilians and armed personnel are inhabiting the same space and area? What consequences would it lead to?" Your answer was: "In armed and military operations, armed personnel may use civilians as for protection, in concrete terms, in street fighting, on combat within settlements, a soldier who may be captured uses civilians to manoeuvre himself out of that particular area is maybe one of the reasons." You realise that you were discussing with counsel at the hypothetical level? Right. Now, I'm rather concerned that a little later you will now make it evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, what am I going to -- you said -- right. At page 42, starting from lines -- line 3 I'll just read the whole paragraph. "Well, in all these actions, to my knowledge, actions of that type, of that type, and fights in villages and towns and cities what is required is to leave some time for the civilians to withdraw. In this specific case, ample time was left for the civilians to withdraw because more than 1500 civilians of Skabrnja withdrew in the direction of Zadar without any consequences. So these civilians either willingly stayed behind or were members or used by members of the ZNG as a human shield. They could have evacuated as well." Now you are testifying, you are no more on a hypothetical level, sir. My question is: Is this your evidence or are you just supposing? Are you speculating that people were used as human shields in this specific case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a presumption. I don't know the real reason, but those civilians who stayed behind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, if it's a presumption, Mr. Milovancevic, I'm sure you'll agree it can't be part of the evidence. We can't move from hypothesis and suddenly make a hypothesis fact. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the presumption on the part of the witness was referred -- was put in response to the Bench's question, not mine. In response to Judge Nosworthy's question, elaborating upon a stance towards civilians, he expressed this presumption. It wasn't in response to my question. I have not finished my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I agree 110 per cent with you, Mr. Milovancevic. Nonetheless, the witness is a Defence witness and I just want to clear this little point with the Defence team as to whether you would accept that in answering the Judges' questions, the witness has moved from a hypothesis and has brought down the hypothesis to what now appears to be evidence and that that is not permissible. I would like -- I would like to get your view on how you expect the Chamber to treat this part of the evidence or this part of the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question by Her Honour Nosworthy was of a principled nature, and the response was partly of a principled nature and partly connected with the specific situation.
