What I'd like to hear, when the Bench examines the witness, then I, as counsel for the Defence, do not control the witness and the witness is in the full jurisdiction of the Bench and the Bench should decide whether additional questions are going to be put to the witness or should the Defence continue. So in this part, I could not lead the -- and examine the witness, so I cannot really answer your question. And in my further re-examination, if it pleases the Bench, I will re-visit this issue so that we could eventually find out whether the witness is hypothesising or whether it refers to reality. I will work up on this thesis furthermore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for His Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. Witness, do you accept that you have moved from a hypothesis to what purports to be testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as the facts in Skabrnja, we can answer a question that was put forward as a hypothesis. But in principle, as regards the principled question, do you read me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In principle, the position and the war customs and laws say that civilians may not be abused as a human shield or for any other purpose. But if a civilian uses weapons and together with a soldier is joined in the same fight or military activities, then they are to be regarded as soldiers. Of course, it has to be proven on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true, but don't add more facts. Here the question just was: A civilian is being used as a human shield, and what would the other side do or what would the other side be expected to do in terms of the laws of war? But I'm happy with your answer. You have said that insofar as it relates to Skabrnja, that was a hypothesis. So I accept that. Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, please, can we get back to your starting point, this sanitization report. What report were you talking about or referring to? We can get that on the screen maybe or learn the number of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, of course. I believe that this would be good in this situation. I am talking about Exhibit 109 is the report prepared by Ernest Radjen on sanitization. It's supposed to be dated 1st of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Questions pertaining to the report of Ernest Radjen are connected with the document that you can see on the screen. Do you recognise that as the document shown by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Under 2, item 2 of this document, reference is made to a 35-year-old man wearing ZNG uniform on the road with a bullet-hole in the area of the head. Under 3 -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under 3, in the courtyard of a privately -- private home, a man, 65-year-old civilian, two women aged 65 to 70, in the basement of a house three elderly people. Under 4, in the courtyard of a private -- two men 25 to 30 years of age in ZNG uniform, one man aged around 60, most probably father and sons, were armed, Kalashnikovs RVM 57, 1-2 Zoljas and most probably hit by shrapnel. One elderly person, woman, in the house. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under 5, in a courtyard of a private home two elderly men, civilians, most probably killed by mines MB, and there is an impact site in the courtyard. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under 7, on the door of one house, one man aged 55, one civilian, two women, 50, 55 years of age in the -- on the ground floor; one woman aged around 70 in the corridor on the first floor. The house was pierced by a shell, most probably a tank shell. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under 9, in an unfinished house on the ground floor three men, one aged between 35 and 40; two men aged around 45; and one female person aged around 55. The youngest man was most probably member of the ZNG. Can you see that under 9?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In item 10, victims are also referred to and the last line reads: One man aged around 40 in the video rental in the ZNG uniform, and that's how item 10 ends. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will refer you to two more items, 12 and 13. Item 12, large garage bearing the sign Andrija Artukovic barracks, containing military equipment, radio-sets, ammunition, ROB, some 30 pieces, three female persons aged around 60 to 65, and one male person aged about 60 in front of the garage, a civilian. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Finally item 13, in the courtyard one female person aged around 60, and in the house two male persons aged around 35, most probably members of the ZNG. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is the question: Does the presence of civilians in the houses where there were armed persons and out of which it was possible to open fire, would that sort of activity from those houses endanger civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions concerning this document. Mr. Lakic, for two days roughly we spoke of the events that took place on the 18th and 19th November, 1991, in Skabrnja, and I'd like to know the following: Did Mr. Martic have any sort of role to play in connection with these events; do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection, Your Honour, this does not arise out of my cross-examination. This is brand new evidence which could have been asked on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If Mr. Prosecutor is not interested in the answer to this question, I will withdraw it, Your Honour. In our -- of course, our position is quite known with regard to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Are you done with your cross-examination -- your re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have one more question, the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When did you leave Krajina and why?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I left Krajina in 1995, specifically on the 4th of August, 1995. I left due to the armed aggression that the Republic of Croatia carried out against the remaining Serb population in Krajina. That was the main sort of reason -- or actually, the only reason at that point in time. The people who had lived in Krajina for centuries left Krajina. It was not the objective of the Serbian people to create a exclusive pure Serb state in territory of Krajina and Croatia. For centuries we had lived together with Croats. In such -- even in such calamity the Serb people wanted to continue living with Croats in the area. However, it was not permitted to do so and the Serb people from the territory of Krajina and Croatia, due to some fabricated positions and force had to leave an area where it had been present for centuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Witness, I have two little questions. First, you mentioned Goran Opacic. Can you tell us if Goran Opacic had a nickname or an alias name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether he had a nickname. He may have had one. I held a relatively high position in the area of Benkovac, and I did not communicate with him by referring to his nickname. We -- I used his full name, but he may have had one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. The full name was, once more? What was the full name?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Opacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't mean you having used the nickname, but maybe you would have known. Then the second question is about the lady commander of the medical unit. What was that name again and how is the family name spelled, please?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Her name was and is Nada Pupovac, P-u-p-o-v-a-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And where was she from or is she from?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, she hails from a village near Benkovac, the village of Perusic. Perusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Do you know where she lives today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today she lives in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those were my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Judge. Mr. Lakic, why were the TOs abolished in November 1992 again?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Territorial Defence was first restructured on the 1st of November, 1991, and there was the TO staff with the local communes and there was the TO brigade under the JNA command. In November of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I'm interested in. In November 1992 ...

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the peace agreement -- agreements under the auspices of the United Nations, the JNA formations no longer existed in the territory of Croatia and Krajina. The border police brigade was established, headquartered in Benkovac, with the sole task of, together with the members of the UN forces, securing the borderline opposite Sibenik and Zadar, or rather, I'm sorry, Biograd and Zadar in the territory of Benkovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- if I can add something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is you have told me nothing about why the TO was abolished in November 1992. I hear what you're telling me here. That doesn't tell me why the TO was abolished in November 1992. Just give me that reason.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the same time, the personnel of the JNA was withdrawn and the Territorial Defence was disbanded as part of the armed forces. The territory of Krajina was covered and controlled by UN forces. That was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Was Darko Miljatovic a member of the Serbian army in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean Darko Miljaljevic, the same person that I mentioned when answering Prosecutor's questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, yes. Oh, it's Mijaljevic, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Darko Mijaljevic was an officer, first of the Territorial Defence and later of the Serbian Army of Krajina through to the end of the war. I think that he ended up with the rank of a captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As of -- I beg your pardon. As of November 1991, of which forces was he a member, the TO or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN LAKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he wasn't a member of the TO forces. I think he was a reserve JNA officer and a commander of special squad or something of the sort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. That concludes my questions. Any questions arising, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: None, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you, Mr. Lakic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. The Chamber would like to thank you for taking the time off to come and testify. Thank you once more. You are excused. You may stand down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, is -- can we go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Next witness, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. You may take a seat. Thank you. Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Madam.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As Defence counsel for the accused, Milan Martic, I will now start my examination-in-chief. As we speak the same language, let us please be mindful of the fact that we have to make a pause between question and answer so that the interpreters can do their job. Can you please tell us your full name.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Nada, nee Pupovac, Drmanic, 10th of March, 1959, in Benkovac, now the Republic of Croatia, previously Yugoslavia, then in Croatia as one federative unit of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what the witness said after her surname. There's something missing after she gives her name. Maybe you could try and get it from her for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, Madam Nosworthy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us once again so that it is stated clearly in transcript your full name?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Nada Drmanic, nee Pupovac, born on the 10th of March, 1959.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That will suffice. What is your ethnicity and your faith, Madam?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Serb and I am of Orthodox faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where precisely is the place where you were born located, what is it called and where is it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I was born in the municipality of Benkovac, in the town of Benkovac. And I lived in Perusic, a village on the outskirts of Benkovac. It is in Northern Dalmatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That will do. Thank you. What is your educational background and where did you work?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I am an administrator by occupation [Realtime transcript read in error "Office of the Prosecution"] and I worked in the Jugoplastika Split company in the Benkovac branch office and in --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat which year she stopped working there for private reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, the interpreter wants to know in which year she stopped for private reasons. I see it says: "I am an administrator by Office of the Prosecution." I want to know if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may put a question concerning this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said that you are by occupation an administrator, specialised in administrative law affairs, does it mean that you completed high school?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. And I worked in the warehouse in the branch office of Jugoplastika in Benkovac for 12 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you worked there until 1990, am I right, and then for private reasons you stopped working there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you worked in the Jugoplastika branch office in the packaging sector. Does it mean that you did not do the job you were in fact schooled for, you did something else?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The village of Perusic, where you resided until 1992, how big is it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It is 2 kilometres long and it has 110 homes, out of which 20 houses were those of Serbs and the rest were Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose that this particular -- this -- the information you gave us dates from 1990?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. In Perusic today, there isn't a single house standing. They weren't destroyed during the aggression, but after the aggression, and I mean the Storm in 1995, they were destroyed in three days following the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the village was inhabited by both Croats and Serbs. Can you tell us something about the inter-ethnic relations there up until 1990.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Until 1990 we lived in an atmosphere of tolerance. There was the maspok, the mass movement in 1971, where there was an attempt to destroy Yugoslavia. And in 1990 the multi-party elections were held where the Croatian Democratic Union won.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will be dealing with that at a later stage. You said that the relations were marked by tolerance, and you mentioned the year 1971. What was it that prompted you to speak of that year?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: In 1971 Ustasha signs and symbols appeared in the village which reminded Serbs to the period between 1941 and 1945 when Ustasha were destroying Serb people and setting up camps. In that period, my family suffered as well. My mother was tied up by combined forces of Ustasha and Germans, which caused her to have a miscarriage. She lost her first child that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know why it was that in 1971 certain problems emerged and how did the Serb population react to them?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The Serbian population organised village guards where men wanted to organise their -- to protect their families. One could hear different songs being chanted to the effect that they were thirsty of Serb blood, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You're speaking of the period marked by the so-called maspok back in 1971. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that the Serbian population back in 1971 stood guard?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why did they organise village guards?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Because the fear of what the Ustashas meant came to life. It was something that had been experienced previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This political process, as you described it, was it brought to a stop? What was life like?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: After that the activity of the services which prompted this movement was halted and tolerance was re-introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you gave us your personal details, you told us where you worked and how long. After this particular employment, did you engage in any social activities, like for instance the youth movement?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I was an active member of the youth movement of Yugoslavia. I was a member of the youth association in the Benkovac municipality. I participated in many social actions and spear-headed many youth labour actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that your village is located in the municipality of Benkovac. What was the make-up of the municipality; do you know?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. The municipality of Benkovac had 51 per cent Serbs and the rest were Croats. There were some Muslims and ethnic Albanians. There were 50 villages, and Benkovac town was 70 per cent Serb; 20 villages were Serb; and two hamlets, Biljane Donje and Trlenje [phoen]; then there were 10 exclusively Croat villages; and 13 mixed villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned interpersonal relationships within your village. Would your characterisation of these relations be valid for the territory of the municipality of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that relations were normal until 1990, do you mean that after 1990 there was a change in these relations?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us when and why.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The multi-party elections in the then-Croatian unit of the Federal Yugoslavia ended by HDZ and Ustasha party taking power. At that point, they wanted to break up Yugoslavia with the help of foreign states that wanted that. HDZ armed their sympathisers. Insignia and symbols re-emerge which did not serve the interest of Yugoslavia. For instance, the flag of the Croatian units within the Federation which was then red, white, and blue with a five-pointed star. But at that time what emerged was the flag, the red, white, and blue, with a chequer-board symbol which revokes Ustasha symbols.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break, which is scheduled for 5.15, I will ask you a brief question. In the first half of 1990, what was the official flag of the federal unit of Croatia within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Official flag was red, white, and blue with the five-pointed star in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if I understood you correctly, flag with the red, white, and blue fields, with a five-pointed star, red star, in the middle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this a fine time to take a break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is the right time indeed, Mr. Milovancevic. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you mentioned 1990 as a year where relations are disturbed. How would this manifest itself in the everyday life in your village, in Benkovac, in Zadar?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the worst case that happened was in May. Member of the Serbian Democratic Party was knifed one evening in the centre of the town. After that, we had cases where families that would move from Benkovac and Zadar would be taken off buses. We had a family of Stegnjaja that was taken off a bus and was later found -- their bodies decapitated and a man's head was put on a woman's body and a woman's head on a man's body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Which period are you referring to. You mentioned the family Stegnjaja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I'm talking about 1990. There were no war activities. It was after the multi-party elections. This all happened in August, and the first case incident happened in May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Stegnjaja family. Could you tell us what happened and how it transpired and where.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were taken off a bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please, between your answers let us make a pause to help the interpretation service. Tell us, please, what happened with the Stegnjaja family.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The Stegnjaja husband was Serb, the woman was a Croat. They were on a bus between Benkovac and Zadar through the place of Zeleni Hrast, which is just beyond Islam Latinski. The bus was stopped by paramilitaries that was created by the HDZ in the then-Yugoslavia. The people on the bus watched Stegnjajas being taken away. Two days later their bodies were found decapitated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The details that you are mentioning, how did you find out about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: My neighbour, an elderly woman, was shocked at the time. She still suffers high blood -- high blood sugar levels and shock because she witnessed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You just said that the first case was in May when somebody was knifed, and the case in hand you are mentioning it took place in September 1990.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please be slower in your responses. So you said they were taken off a bus. Where would they -- where were they taken away?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Their bodies were found in some bushes by the roadside, and they were buried at the Kasic cemetery, the village of Kasic in Ravni Kotari. Even their remains were not laid in peace because their bones were disinterred and the tombstones were broken down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the event. These people were murdered?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the husband and wife had their heads severed and that the woman's head was placed on the husband's body and vice versa. Is that what you're testifying to?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the surname of these people?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Stegnjaja, the Stegnjaja family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the local population to these events?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Of course they were upset, distressed at -- during that period in the summertime police station in Benkovac had target -- been target of an attempt to disarm and then Serbs would be without protection in the Benkovac area, because HDZ were -- had control over paramilitary formations and wanted to appoint their armed staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Would -- did this incident have ramifications of everyday life in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, of course it had. People could not commute to work. People could not sleep. Village guards had to be organised. There was much trepidation because many people had survived World War II under Ustasha occupation and suffered the emblems of the chequer-board.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does Cirkovic Tomislav ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that was the man who was married in my village two houses down the road from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. The period of August/September, of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What do you associate this person and this wedding?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Because this was the first time that armed people took part in the wedding ceremonies. I could not move around the village for the first time because I was held at gun-point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I'm not quite sure we are getting a mistranslation. You're talking about a wedding, and the witness hadn't spoken about a wedding according to the transcript. How does it come in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did mention --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask a number of questions to elaborate upon this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Tomislav Cirkovic --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It's not Cirkovic but Curkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is when facts come from your side for the first time before they've been mentioned by the witness. I don't mind you asking a few questions, but, you know, let's get the testimony from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since I was listening to the witness, let me ask a few questions so that we avoid a situation where I would be leading the witness or I would be testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So the name of this man Curkovic, what event do you associate with that name in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: At his wedding ceremony, all members of the HDZ had -- were -- had Kalashnikovs. They were firing rounds and to prove that they were armed. At the same evening, they blocked the road towards Benkovac and they held me at gun-point and returned me back home. I couldn't reach Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that that person lived two houses down the road from your house in the village and he was married that day. Who toted Kalashnikovs and how did you find out that they had Kalashnikovs?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I could see it from my house. The wedding guests were members of the HDZ, which transpired afterwards because everybody knows everybody else in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there rounds fired and why, on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank God not at us, and they blocked the Benkovac-Perusic road which leads to Kolarina which is a major Serb inhabited village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What were your feelings about that event?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you can't really be indifferent when somebody held you at gun-point and inserts a round into the barrel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the mention of "redarstvenici" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, in the -- there's "redarstvenici," disarmed policemen in Benkovac. They were left without weapons. Two redarstvenici, Sisgora and Curkovic, lived in my village. They lived there and commuted under arms in full combat gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Am I much mistaken if I say that you are referring to the second part of 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm referring to summer, August and September of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the term "redarstvenik" mean at that time, what it referred to?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It referred to an Ustasha soldier of HDZ's paramilitary formations in the then-country of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were two such lads who joined the redarstvenici or police formations from your village?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, Sisgora and Curkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You were -- you said you were -- they were armed. What kind of arms?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Automatic rifles, bombs, grenades, whichever was part of the set-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did they wear?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: In camouflage fatigues, as any other soldier. They wore the insignia of the Ustashi army with an Ustashi emblem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the time in autumn of 1990, the mention of the textile factory in Vuksic, does it mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I was seeking employment, and I was told that in Vuksic it would really be -- well, at the time it was really hard to find a job. And they told me that the factory in Vuksic had vacancies. First you had Vuksic, a Serb village, then -- first you had Kolarina, a Serb village, and then Vuksic, a mixed village, and there they had a textile factory. As I entered the premises of the factory, I came across a scene which harked back to the Ustasha rule. I saw thousands and thousands of flags on the premises. At first, I couldn't make out which flags they were. I realised that they were not the official flags of the Socialist Republic of Croatia, which existed in the then-Yugoslavia. These were Ustasha flags sporting the Ustasha sign, that of a chequer-board. I turned around and left the area without pursuing my intention to get employed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you to say that you went to that textile factory with the intention of getting a job there, but that as soon as you saw the flags you gave up the idea?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Does the mention of barricades ring a bell in this first half of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the first barricade that was erected in my village was in the month of October during the grapes harvest. One was erected in front of my house at the end of the village, and this meant that we no longer were able or free to go through the Croat part of the village. The barricade was erected by a man, a villager, I personally knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did the barricade consist of?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Those were disused car tires. From that date on, unknown people, members of the HDZ, started coming to the village and holding meetings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As of the period when the barricades were erected, did you go to Zadar and what about the other villagers?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I myself did not go to Zadar, but the Serbs who lived in other parts of Croatia and who were native of the area of Benkovac started returning to Benkovac because back where they lived they were asked to sign loyalty oaths to the Croatian authorities. Their houses were destroyed. We know that in Zadar more than 140 dwellings were destroyed, some of those were residential homes, others were business premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there, please. You made two points now, one was the loyalty oaths, as you call them. Who asked whom to sign these loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It was the party that won the majority of seats, the HDZ, who had their own followers in all the businesses, and they asked employees to sign such loyalty oaths. Those who would not sign them had to leave that particular area because they were afraid that night-time would engulf them or that they would just simply disappear. My own family went through a similar type of torture in 1991. I haven't seen that part of my family for 16 years now and haven't been in touch with them all because of cases such as the one I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that people were required sign loyalty oaths. Did it mean that whoever signed such loyalty oaths at one's work-place would remain in employment?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: No, no. Even those people who signed such oaths did not stay there because they were forced out of their homes so that other people who never lived there could move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You've just told us that there were people who signed loyalty oaths, but still this wasn't enough. They were moved out of their homes. By whom?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: By the HDZ authorities who styled themselves or posed as the regular authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, why did the people who signed loyalty oaths to the HDZ have to leave? Why were they expelled?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Because they were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I will appeal to you again to make a short pause before answering my questions because we will -- this will prove too taxing on the interpreters. You've just told us that people were terribly frightened of the repercussions of not signing such oaths. Why?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were afraid that they would be killed. The Ustasha authorities did not -- were not too selective about the means that they employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have taken the solemn declaration and you are testifying to certain events. You say that those who would not sign such loyalty oaths at their work-places were exposed to the danger, to the threat, of being killed. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who would kill them, the people who didn't sign loyalty oaths?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The HDZ authorities headed by Franjo Tudjman, who was alive at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that those who refused to sign such oaths were very much afraid. What did they do next?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They went back to the municipality of Benkovac. They had to leave their place of residence under pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The people who went back to the municipality of Benkovac, what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Serb, and we had one ethnic Italian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Just on the point of interest, did you have any Croats who refused to sign oaths to the HDZ who were asked to sign oaths? Did any refuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any such knowledge. I don't have any information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The events you've been describing took place in 1990. I'm interested in what the situation was like in 1991. In the area of Benkovac, were there any JNA units and were there any such units in Dalmatia?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Sir, there had to be the Yugoslav People's Army since that was the army of the state that existed at the time, the sovereign and internationally recognised state.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the situation like in mid-1991 concerning the JNA in the area?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: In all the areas where Croats were in the majority, the JNA came under attacks, its members were being killed and captured. They had to find ways to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the JNA at the time?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did you come by the information?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: A unit was being pulled out of Zadar into Benkovac which was commanded by Perisic, and he himself and his unit had been in Zadar encircled and without water-supplies for a long time. The Zemunik airport, it was encircled for a long time, under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far the Zemunik airport is from Benkovac and also the distance between Zadar and Benkovac.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The distance between Zadar and Benkovac is about 30 kilometres, I believe, whereas the airport and Zadar are some 4 kilometres away. The first village, a mixed Croat/Serb village, is Zemunik Donje and then Skabrnja. The road to Benkovac is across Biljane Donje -- or, rather, Skabrnja, Biljane Donje, and Zemunik Gornje, the Croat part all the way to Smiljcic. All these roads were blocked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: These are all roads leading to and from the Zemunik airport. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. These were the roads that were being used, and they all converge at Zemunik Donje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the roads leading to and from Zemunik were blocked, can you tell us who effected the blockades and how.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The blockades were set up by Croats and their paramilitary forces. The main points from which they could control not only the airport but also the Benkovac-Biljane road and Benkovac-Biljane Gornje road toward the Ravni Kotor villages and the Biograd-Benkovac road was Razovljeva Glava. From Nadinska Gradina one could also control a large area, and from there 60-millimetre mortars were used to fire upon Benkovac, and I'm speaking about the vantage point of Nadinska Gradina, and the distance is some 3 to 4 kilometres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did you get this information from? Where did you get all these details concerning Razovljeva Glava, Nadinska Kosa, the events at Benkovac and Zemunik?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I was a member of the Territorial Defence in Benkovac under the command of Mr. Zoran Lakic. I was the commander of the medical corps, and I held the post at the time when both roads leading to the Zemunik airport were supposed to be -- got rid of the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the TO, what were your specific duties?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: At the time, my task was -- or, rather, let me explain this in greater detail. I was a member of the civilian protection when I worked for my company, and I went through Red Cross training and thereupon I took part in various exercises. This is how I came to be involved in the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you went -- attended various Red Cross courses and took part in exercises and competitions and that this was how you came to be involved in the TO. So would I be wrong in inferring that you were a nurse within the TO forces?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: No, you wouldn't be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the Territorial Defence, specifically as a member of the medical corps, you said that you belonged to the unit under the command of Mr. Zoran Lakic?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that it was in this capacity that you took part in two attempts to lift the blockade of Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us when the first attempt took place and what happened.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: On the 30th of September, 1991, there was this first attempt from the direction of Devici to enter Nadin peacefully with a view to lifting the siege of Nadinska Glava and freeing the road leading to the airport, to open up food-supplies and so on. At the time the army had already been withdrawing from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. At that point in time, on the 30th of September, 1991, who led the action of deblocking Nadinska Glava?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It was the JNA, the army of the country that was in existence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you come to be involved in the action?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: As soon as the JNA set off toward Nadin from Devici it came across land-mines. There were anti-tank mines, personnel mines, and trip mines. A tank came across a tank mine. There were people wounded. One of the JNA members got killed. I was pulling out those wounded from the tank with my team, and I got into a minefield in the process. We managed to pull out, but that was where we had to stop. We couldn't advance. A soldier by the name of Strbac got killed. There was shelling at the airport. The first victim was Svetozar Cubrilo. He got killed in the shelling that came from the direction of Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the JNA set off toward Nadinska Glava, that a tank came across a mine --

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And that you actually set off to assist them.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You spoke of the tank mines, personnel, and trip mines. How did you come to know about that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I found myself in the middle of a minefield as I was trying to pull out two of the crewmen out of a tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us and describe for us how it was.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: As I set out, I didn't expect as many minefields to be there. But later on it turned out that the Benkovac-facing side was laid with mines, completely. I'm not speaking of Nadinska Kosa, of the high ground there, I'm speaking of the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Pause there. You said that the [indiscernible] side up to the road was mined. Who did lay the mines?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Paramilitary forces of Croatia, of today's Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did you manage to reach the destroyed tank and how did you pull them out and how did you get out of the minefield?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I had to stop until after the sappers have cleared the minefield so that we can pull out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Were there people injured in the tank?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, two. One lost a leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Whose was this tank, of which army was that soldier?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Of the Yugoslav army, both the tank and the soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you at that time -- or, better said, which unit did you belong to, JNA or the TO?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: To the TO, but they were under the command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On the 30th of September, 1991, when you were approaching Nadinska Kosa, apart from coming across minefields were there any fire opened at you?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: There was fierce fire fighting. The army wanted to avoid casualties because those involved were citizens of Yugoslavia and in the ranks of JNA there were Slovenes, Siptars, Muslims, Hungarians, et cetera. The fact was that the tank unit was commanded by Stjepan Rekenji.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who opened fire and from where, opened fire against the unit of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Fire was opened by the paramilitary unit residing at Nadin at the time --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction: Paramilitary unit of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the end result?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Military retreated to their base. Later on the situation was attempted to be resolved, the situation with the airport by an attempt to negotiate a way from Zemunik through Skabrnja, but that attempt failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us how did you learn about a peaceful attempt on the 30th of September? Who is the source of that information? You said that the JNA set out in tanks and you referred to it as a peaceful attempt. Could you describe that?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA, it was much more powerful than they were. They could neutralise them, but they did not want to bring about casualties in their own people so they retreated because they wanted to find a peaceful solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You just said that you took part twice in the action aimed at lifting the blockade of the airport in the direction of Skabrnja. When was this second attempt?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The second attempt was on the 18th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us, when did you learn that this action is going to take place, how did you learn about that, and briefly describe your involvement in that action.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: There were no special preparations. I was notified to be on stand-by, that I will be stationed at Trljuge, hamlet of Biljane Donje village. We were ordered to be on stand-by if there were any casualties or to help with any possible evacuation of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us who said that and when?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Zoran Lakic told me that because he maintained radio communication with me on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zoran Lakic as the commander of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, commander of the Territorial Defence of Benkovac told you to be ready for the 18th November, 1991, because of the forthcoming action?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go and with whom? How did it all start and when on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: A unit of the JNA and the Territorial Defence of Benkovac set out jointly to lift the blockade of the Zemunik airport from Trljuge down the road which leads to the airport and en route through Zemunik Donje they advanced. We stayed behind in Trljuge. That's a hamlet of Biljane Donje. And after half an hour, Lieutenant Stefanovic could be heard. He was speaking into a bull-horn and we could hear it because it was close by. He tried to appeal for the road to be cleared; in response, we heard machine-gun fire. And then we were notified that we should go to the hamlet of Ambar within the village of Skabrnja. I set out in a blue van marked with a red cross through the Croatian part of the Zemunik Gornje village. People were on the their balconies, on terraces, both young and old. Nobody offered any resistance, as it was planned peacefully. But when I reached Ambar I was met with a terrible scene. Lieutenant Stefanovic had been killed and a soldier, I believe Samir was his name, he was a Muslim, tried to help him and was hit right next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you heard gun-fire and you were summoned. Who summoned you and by which means?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: By radio communication, both Lakic and the JNA, Yugoslav People's Army, that was situated at Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately when was it when you reached the hamlet of Ambar and when you were met with the situation where Lieutenant Stefanovic and Muslim soldier Samir were killed?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The action started at 7.00 and it -- I was there in ten minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you received the call and when you heard machine-gun fire to come to Ambar you were, as you said, at the hamlet Trljuge. What is the distance between the two places?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Maybe 300 metres, not -- even less as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you said you reached to Ambar, was there fire going on or was it peaceful?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: There was still fire-fights. They shot at me as well, although I wore an armband, white armband with the Red Cross symbol, and I had a bag with me with material. And they -- I came across young soldiers who were in tears because they were shocked by the death of that lieutenant. They were very fond of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I forgot to ask you something. I will do that now. You said that you set out into that action as a member of the TO, as a member of the medical corps. You mentioned a blue van?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How many people of the medical corps were there? What was your uniform? What was your equipment?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: There were three women within the medical corps and one man who drove the van. We had a stretcher in the van. We had bags, first aid bags, and everything else was done by an out-patient clinic at Smiljcic. Unfortunately, the woman who is now incarcerated in Croatian prisons is there without justification because she never set foot in Skabrnja. She was convicted of the crimes in Skabrnja, Ms. Banic never saw Skabrnja, and she's now incarcerated in Croatian prisons, as opposed to me who was in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You answered something that you were not asked about, but since you mentioned it, you mentioned that there were three women in the medical corps and the driver, a man. And you said that Madam Banic was convicted?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: In absentia she was convicted and sentenced to 20 years in prison. When she was re-tried, she was handed down a sentence of 13, then 10 years. I witnessed via videolink from Belgrade, and finally she was convicted and sentenced to six years in prison, but it's unfair because even six minutes prison sentence is too long if a person is innocent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. Let's close the book on this issue. You said that: "Ms. Banic was not with me and she was convicted." What does it mean? She was convicted for allegedly being in Skabrnja. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: She was accused of killing people in Skabrnja. This is terrible. We were not in the service of any military to kill; we were there to help people, be it Serbs, Croats, Muslims, Turks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "we were there to help people," are you referring to yourself and Ms. Banic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nada Drmanic and Ms. Banic is in Croatian prison right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your remark makes me suspect you didn't understand me. My question was simply: Were you there helping people with Ms. Banic in Skabrnja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, sir. You understood me right. Ms. Banic was not in Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said, sir [as interpreted], how many people was the medical unit composed of. Could you tell us how many soldiers on the part of the JNA took part in this action, do you know that, and what resources were sent there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: As far as I could see, but I cannot tell you a specific number, I wasn't a JNA officer. There was some 200 soldiers in all, infantry, tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you reached the Ambar hamlet, could you describe what were your actions then. How did you establish that the lieutenant and the soldier were killed?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I was there, and I felt his pulse. There was no pulse. And my team drove him to Smiljcic, and other teams took over from there. I remained there because it was difficult to approach this area because of the fire opened by the Croatian side. I stayed there because it was -- be easier for me to provide help, assistance, and aid, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you pulled out the killed lieutenant of the JNA, Stefanovic. Where did you pull him out from?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: He was on the APC, on the road towards Skabrnja 50 metres into the hamlet of Ambar. There were several anti-tank mines that had been dismantled by the time that the medical unit reached that spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: For the Bench and the Prosecutor to understand what it is all about and for me to be clear, could you explain what was this APC.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: That's armoured personnel carrier, military armoured personnel carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Was it inside or outside?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Outside. When he was killed, he was hit in the neck. He was the one who appealed for peaceful agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you find the killed soldier?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Next to lieutenant. Because that soldier tried to help the lieutenant, but that Croatian side shot and hit him as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: That soldier was next to the killed lieutenant. Where were they? I apologise if I'm asking silly questions.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were on the APC on the road towards Skabrnja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I ask you these questions because I am not supposed to put to you leading questions. I've just heard from you that the killed lieutenant was on the APC and that the soldier was on that APC next to the lieutenant. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who pulled these people out? You, yourself, or were you assisted by anybody?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: My team and I and a soldier, Mr. Boksic, a Croat, was among those soldiers. That Boksic came from Makarska and we knew that because his cousin is a well-known footballer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm not sure if the witness said she pulled them out of the APC. Wasn't it that you said that in your question? Witness, can you describe that once more, where were these people. In the translation I got it said "on the APC. We pulled them out" or so, but this was then already answering the question. Can you describe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we reached that spot, we found people trying to pull them out of the APC, but because of the intense firing on the part of the Croatian side it was difficult to take them out. We did what we can -- could. We pulled them out of the APC, tried to provide them with first aid, but they had already died because neither of them had any pulse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: So they were in the APC and still they were killed? Isn't this an armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I've made myself quite clear. They were in the APC, but jutting out of the APC was the lieutenant holding the megaphone and calling on to the other side to reach an agreement. However, the other side, the Croatian paramilitaries, did not respond peacefully. They returned fire and hit the lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: But, Witness, it's not necessary to say you made yourself quite clear. If there is a question, there is a question, apparently it's then not so clear. And I'm not sure clear in that one point now. What did you see? Did you see the lieutenant speaking through the megaphone? Then you can describe the position he took. Otherwise, it's maybe something you heard. Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I and all of us who were present in the area heard him speak over the megaphone because that's how loud it was. Now, the soldiers who were there told me how the things happened. They were near the APC, and we arrived quite soon because we were stationed nearby. It didn't take us long to reach the spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I want to make one thing clear to you. We don't know what happened there and have to establish precisely how things happened. Sometimes things appear clearly; other times they don't. And please answer our questions because we want to arrive at what actually happened there. That is the point of the whole exercise. Thank you. Let me ask you the following. In view of the description you gave us - and with this I will try to end this line of questioning - were the lieutenant and the soldier partly in the APC and partly outside of it?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is my next question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I thought the witness said earlier, Mr. Milovancevic, that it was the lieutenant who was jutting out of the APC. You didn't say that about the other soldier. I'm not sure whether now are we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see what you mean. Allow me to put several questions to clarify this. I've put a great deal of questions to the witness and perhaps managed to confuse her in the process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you haven't managed to confuse her. You're managing to confuse the Chamber, Mr. Milovancevic. The problem is that you put words into the mouth of witnesses, and I've tried to warn you against this. The witness said at page 81, line 22 to 25: "Sir, I've made myself quite clear. They were in the APC, but jutting out of the APC was the lieutenant holding the megaphone and calling on to the other side to reach an agreement. However, the other side, the Croatian paramilitaries, did not respond peacefully. They returned fire and hit the lieutenant." Now, there's nothing confusing and confused about that statement; it's quite clear. Now, when you suggest to the witness that the soldier was also jutting out, you are testifying. So please phrase your questions in question form; don't tell her something to agree with. Ask her the question and let her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're quite right. In view of the answer you've just read out, my last question was quite superfluous, and I -- this answer of the witness has kind of slipped out of my attention and that wasn't my intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Where were the JNA soldiers stationed or placed as you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were next to the APC, and this is in Dalmatia where you had walls there and they would seek shelter behind them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you established that both of those killed had no pulse?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: A short lull ensued, and at around 12.00 when they - and when I say "they," I mean the Croatian side - resumed fire, the Yugoslav army had to fire back. They had to protect themselves because they were pitted against paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said it took you some ten minutes to arrive there. You pulled the men out. What was the conduct of the JNA? How did the other side behave? When did the fighting end?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: A half an hour later on there was a lull, but then at 12.00 they opened fire against the JNA once more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As soon as the firing stopped for the first time, where were the JNA soldiers, those you administered medical assistance, to?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were in the shelters that they were able to find. You had those stone walls along the road, and that was the only shelter that they could use because the army was along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: From which direction did the fire come that hit the JNA?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: From the area of Razovljeva Glava and they had support from Prkos, Zemunik Donje and Galovci. So they had infantry fire coming from Razovljeva Glava and they had artillery support from these other locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the forces in Skabrnja had artillery support from Prkos and Galovci?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who provided the support?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The Croatian paramilitaries again. Those were Croat villages below Skabrnja, Zemunik Donje, Galovci, and Prkos, those were the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that the forces in Skabrnja had artillery support, what does it mean in actual fact? What was the target of the artillery fire from Zemunik Donje, Galovci, and Prkos?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Their target was purportedly the JNA. What they did in actual fact was to also fire upon the houses of their own people, because it wasn't always the case that they in fact hit the target. Shells fell all over the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after you evacuated the two persons who were killed, half an hour later there was a lull. Did your unit withdraw from the area or not? What happened on the other side?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: I stayed behind whilst my team went away transporting the two killed. I stayed there because I didn't want to expose myself to fire and I wanted to be there close at hand to assist any wounded, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that after 12.00 fire was resumed. Who opened fire and upon whom?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: It was the Croatian paramilitaries who opened fire upon the JNA soldiers, soldiers of the country that existed. The JNA naturally returned fire. Under the constitution and law, in such situation, the attacked side is entitled to defend itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What did the JNA do? What happened? Can you briefly describe that.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The army came under fire from all houses. It was hard to tell where the fire came from. The fire came from the bell-tower of the church from Razovljeva Glava. The artillery support also opened fire and the army of course had to neutralise the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the army came under fire and that it responded. Which JNA forces were in Skabrnja at the time?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, the JNA had infantry troops who returned fire, and tanks also opened fire in the direction of Galovci from where artillery fire came upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the tanks were placed along the road and foot soldiers - and I mean the JNA soldiers - where were they?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: They were behind -- sheltered behind the wall alongside the road. Those were the walls of the courtyards of the houses along the road which could best be used as shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the JNA soldiers come off the road during the fighting?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know why this was the case?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Those were their orders, and the goal was to avoid any casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the fighting resumed at 12.00. What happened then? Did you move forward?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, we were moving along the road in Skabrnja. There were bodies of those dead and wounded civilians, and we started pulling out and evacuating wounded Croats. I pulled out two -- three or four old men. I pulled out a young man who was wounded; I believe his name was Ivica. I dressed his wounds and pulled him out. There were also dead civilians there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: May we learn what that means, "pulled civilians out," out of where? Where was that? What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Pull out," well that's the term we used in wartime. This meant that we pulled persons out of the combat zone. In this specific case, these were villagers whom I took toward the van and transported them on to Smiljcic where they would be provided further medical assistance. Now, as for the dead civilians, I don't know who pulled them out. Whoever was alive and wounded was taken by us to Smiljcic, where they would be provided further aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now, when you say that you gave medical assistance to people, were there any JNA soldiers wounded there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the action of pulling out the wounded involved.

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I had to pull out persons, be it a Serb, Muslim, or Croat, whilst being exposed to fire. I was pulling the persons behind the walls where I took shelter, and then tried to somehow place them on my back and drag them to the van. We came under fire, the van came under fire, despite the fact that it had the red cross mark on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: With regard to this, I have a specific question. You see a wounded person in front of you. In what way do you approach the people and what do you do next? Were you alone or did you have the assistance of someone else?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, you see, first of all I had to hurl myself into shrubbery there, so as not to be hit. And then, as I would try to reach the wounded person, I would have to pull down a part of the wall to actually get hold of the person. It was horrific.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: The wounded you pulled out were transported to Smiljcic, you say?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Why there?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: We had a physician there who was able to provide them with adequate medical assistance and, where necessary, the persons were further transported to the hospital in Knin in order for shrapnel to be extracted or for any other surgery to be carried out. This was something I had nothing to do with anymore. My duty was to pull the person out of the combat zone and provide -- administer aid as far as I was able to. The rest had to be done by the physician.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the wounded civilians you assisted, what of the other civilians you came across in the village?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: The civilians mingled with the MUP members, ZNG members, the members of 159th Brigade or whichever brigade they were. They were mingling with the civilians in the cellars of the houses. You couldn't tell who was a civilian or who wasn't. Every able-bodied man in Skabrnja carried a weapon, carried a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what do you base in statement of yours on?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I myself saw civilians shooting out -- firing out of houses and they would throw their own civilians out of these cellars, out of these homes, in order to protect their own lives. Another person stated as much. This was a person who was a disabled. He was in wheelchair, and I provided him some food that evening. And he said that there was this one man who did not allow civilians to be pulled out of the village. His name was Miljanic. He wouldn't allow them to be evacuated from the village. Instead, he forced them to come into harm's way, into the fire. They even killed a family there because they wanted to negotiate with the army. As much was told to me by a man who was in a wheelchair. I believe he was a police officer before that. He wasn't that old, but he was an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: We've come to the end of day, but let us just clarify who was this man who was bound to the wheelchair? Where was he from?

utterances.speaker: NADA PUPOVAC
utterances.text: He was a villager from Skabrnja, an invalid, who was bound to his wheelchair. We protected him, took him out of the combat zone, and provided him some food that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe, Your Honour, that we have finished for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Ma'am, we have come to the end of the day. Will you please be -- make sure that you are back in court tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon so that we can continue with your evidence. For the time being, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. There's just one little housekeeping matter here that we need to deal with. The Trial Chamber will now renders its decision on two Defence motions concerning Witness MM-105. On the 16th of October, 2006, the Defence filed a motion for the admission into evidence of the statement of Witness MM-105 pursuant to Rule 92 ter. In its written response of the 26th of October, 2006, the Prosecution did not object to the admission of this statement. The Trial Chamber orders that the statement of Witness MM-105 be admitted into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter subject to the witness: (a) appearing in court for cross-examination and any questioning by the Judges; and (b) attesting that the statement accurately reflects his declaration and what he would say if examined in chief in court. Further, the Trial Chamber orders the Defence counsel to place -- I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. Further, the Trial Chamber orders the registrar to place the statement of Witness MM-105 under seal and orders the Defence to file a redacted public statement by expunging the following paragraphs: 3, 20, 22, 23, 30, 35, 38, 40, 47, 48, and 49. On the 16th of October, the Defence filed a motion requesting the protective measures of pseudonym and closed session for Witness MM-105. In its written response of 30th of October, 2006, the Prosecution did not oppose the protective measures of pseudonym and, if requested, image and voice distortion; however, the Prosecution objects to the use of closed session for this witness. The Defence submits that Witness MM-105, who regularly travels to Croatia, would fear for his safety while in Croatia if it became known that he testified. The Trial Chamber considers that the risk to Witness MM-105's security asserted by the Defence may rightly be described as very low and finds that pseudonym will be the appropriate protective measure. The registrar is ordered to assign a pseudonym to Witness MM-105. With regard to the request for closed session, the Trial Chamber finds that the Defence has not shown an objectively grounded risk to the witness's or the witness's family's security or welfare. The Trial Chamber reminds the parties that closed session is an extraordinary measure of witness protection. Therefore, there is a more onerous obligation upon the requesting party to establish the risk asserted. The personal circumstances of Witness MM-105, as expressed by the Defence, do not meet this standard. The request for closed session for Witness MM-105 is therefore denied. Should the Defence wish to apply for other protective measures in relation to this witness, it should do so in writing by 12.00 tomorrow, submitting further reasons for such a request. Thank you. That brings us to the end of the order and also the end of the day. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in Courtroom II, this same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 31st day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 24 25
